idiom_name: Thread#thread_variable_get/set (true thread-local), Thread#[] (fiber-local), Fiber storage (3.2+), Ractor isolation
implementation_notes: Ruby splits the concept in two: `Thread.current.thread_variable_set/get` are genuinely thread-scoped, while `Thread#[]`/`Thread#[]=` are fiber-local despite the historical name - a distinction that bites on fiber-based servers and inside lazy enumerators. Since Ruby 3.2 `Fiber#storage`/`Fiber[]` provides inheritable request-local state that is copied into child fibers/threads (the feature explicitly designed to replace blind thread-local copying by frameworks), and Ractors go further: state inside a Ractor is isolated and only frozen/shareable data may cross. The confinement discipline is unchanged - no reference to a confined object may be stored anywhere another thread or fiber can reach it; the GVL makes single-threaded access fast but does not prevent a leaked reference from corrupting state. Choose `thread_variable_*` for genuinely thread-affine resources and `Fiber[]` for request context.
code_sketch:
Thread.current.thread_variable_set(:fmt, Formatter.new)  # thread-local
fmt = Thread.current.thread_variable_get(:fmt)           # this thread only

Thread.current[:req_id]      # fiber-local, NOT thread-local
Fiber[:request_id] = id      # Ruby 3.2+: inherited by child fibers/threads
Ractor.new { work }          # ractors share no mutable objects at all
pitfalls: `Thread.current[:key]` is fiber-local: code running inside a Fiber (lazy enumerators, async gem tasks, Falcon) does not see values set outside it.
Thread-locals are never cleaned from long-lived worker threads; pools accumulate stale per-request data, which is precisely why Fiber storage was introduced with explicit inheritance semantics.
Ractors raise isolation errors when a non-shareable object crosses a boundary - that is confinement working, but code relying on globals breaks loudly and must be redesigned around messages.
